Q: How do I get typing to work on generic class when creating a property with a function? A:

This is a bit more complicated that you might thing since in python isinstance(object,type) is as true as isinstance(type,object). You have 3 possible ways to solve this:

  • Make a unique call to use when "type" checking : class Foo: def mytype(self):return self.identifier; in which you are basically having your own function to return the identifier which can be int, string, bitfield whatever. So instead of using isinstance(xcls,type) or isinstance(xobj,cls) youd simply use your method instead.
  • Make class which holds value of varying kinds with serialisation, sanitisation and verification included and simply store any value in that class instance. This is done with property class, since in python property is simply a class isinstance(property,object) should yield True.
  • Go deep into python metaclassing and interfacing. Basically in Cpython it has varying ways to construct object and type , but python itself allows us to do metaclassing, such as class MyType(type): pass to make your own type, and then class MyObj(metaclass=MyType):pass to make an class constructed from that type.

Basically, type is checked via consistent python provided interface of method resolution order which is exposed via __dunder__ methods and attributes that global / builtin functions take advantage of. That way builtins.len might invoke cls.__len__ method or any other fallback, which happens trough series of interfaces that one define within type or object to be used by those functions.

But no one has to use that, and can simply make their own function or method to do similar stuff. The way one does this can span from simply developing method to call, attribute to return, interaction between master and slave (ie property) classes or make their own type. Mind you that making your own type comes with their own difficulties and unless specifically required to, Id suggest going trough progression method->property->class->type.

Q: Err.Raise() is ignoring custom description and source A:

I had the same problem. I figured out that the behaviour changed when the instance of the error raising class was typed explicitly. So if you change the type of your class to variant you should keep your custom error message:

Sub TestSub()
  Dim Example As Variant   'use Variant instead of Test to keep your custom error message
  Set Example = New Test

  On Error GoTo errorHandler
  Example.Value = -1
  On Error GoTo 0
  Exit Sub

errorHandler:
  MsgBox Err.Number & "," & Err.Description & " in " & Err.Source
End Sub

Q: How to use __has_include correctly? A:

I frequently add a #pragma message or #warning to see what path the preprocessor took (especially when I am testing). in this case I would add a message to the X11 case for the __has_include and also add an else path with a message. printing the value of __STDC_VERSION may also be helpful.

this suggestion may not explain why it did not work but at least there would be feedback to show what it actually did.

Q: Can the next-generation Intel compiler add code-paths for multiple instruction sets? A:

Yes — this is supported in newer versions of the Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ compiler.

The -ax option is available for generating multiple feature-specific code paths in a single binary, with runtime dispatch selecting the appropriate implementation for the CPU.

For example:

icx -axSKYLAKE-AVX512,BROADWELL source.cpp

According to Intel's current compiler documentation, -ax generates additional optimized code paths when there is a performance benefit, while keeping a compatible baseline path.

So the issue in the question appears to be related to the older 2022.0/2022.0.1 compiler versions, where this functionality was not yet supported by the LLVM-based compiler.

Updating to a newer oneAPI DPC++/C++ compiler should provide the behaviour that the classic Intel compiler previously offered.

Intel docs:
https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/dpcpp-cpp-compiler/developer-guide-reference/2025-0/ax-qax.html

Q: How to use data returned by an INSERT...RETURNING in another query? A:

MariaDB doesn't support data modifying CTEs, so you can't use INSERT ... RETURNING inside a WITH clause and then use the result in another query like you can in PostgreSQL.

For an ON DUPLICATE KEY case, one common workaround is:

INSERT INTO my_table (...)
VALUES (...)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = LAST_INSERT_ID(id);

Then LAST_INSERT_ID() gives you the existing row's id when the row already exists.
